title: Tenant Isolation Economics and Fallback Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary

This playbook describes the economics, architecture, and operational runbook for tenant isolation (soft and hard) across Redwood's serving platform. It is intended for platform engineers, SREs, and product owners who need to balance isolation guarantees, cost efficiency, and graceful degradation. The guidance below codifies: isolation modes, billing/chargeback signals, safe fallback chains, SLO/alert thresholds, autoscaling and eviction policies, rollout steps, and post-incident retrospective checklist.

Goals

- Provide deterministic latency and throughput guarantees for high-priority tenants with bounded cost exposure.
- Reduce noisy-neighbor impact with predictable eviction mechanics and verified fallback behavior.
- Expose clear chargeback signals so product/finance can trade isolation vs unit economics.
- Ensure any isolation action has an automatic, observable, and reversible fallback path.

Scope

Applies to: Redwood Dedicated and Hosted inference runtime. Not intended for Private (customer-managed) deployments beyond the recommended knobs.

Terminology

- Hard isolation: physical or reserved GPU pools with no overcommit.
- Soft isolation: logical tenant slices sharing pools with prioritization, preemption and burst credits.
- Burst credit: pre-allocated budget allowing short bursts above baseline QPS.
- Fallback model: lower-cost/quantized model variant used when primary capacity is unavailable.

Architecture and design patterns

Key services and signals:
- router-service: request routing, tenant tag enrichment, tokenized cost meter.
- scheduler-orch: slice allocation, eviction, burst bookkeeping.
- kv-prefix-cache: prefix (KV) cache for hot contexts (per-tenant TTL).
- autoscaler: scale-up/scale-down decisions for Dedicated pools.

Isolation modes and recommended usage:

1) Reserved (Hard)
- Use when latency SLO <= 50ms P95 and no >5% tail deviation allowed.
- Minimum pool size: 2 GPUs for HA.
- Billing: monthly reserved capacity charge + usage surcharge for >commit spikes.

2) Priority Slice (Soft)
- Use when latency SLO <= 150ms P95 and tenant can tolerate brief degradation.
- Baseline share + burst credits (config example below).

3) Best-effort
- For development, evaluation, or low-cost tiers. No SLA.

Cost model (example)

| Component | Unit | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Reserved GPU hour | $2.40 | 8x A100 equivalent (example) |
| Token compute cost | $0.0000012 | per-token normalized unit |
| Burst credit unit | $0.05 | consumed per 10s above baseline |

Chargeback signals exposed to customers via Console (examples):
- reserved_capacity_committed_gpus
- burst_credit_balance (per-tenant)
- average_token_cost_24h

Configuration examples

YAML: priority slice with burst credits

slice_config:
  name: "priority-payments"
  baseline_qps: 50
  burst_credits: 1200 # 12 minutes of 10x burst
  fallback_policy:
    - type: "model_variant"
      order: ["redwood-2-quant","redwood-2-int8","redwood-1-small"]
    - type: "degrade_latency_target"
      max_added_latency_ms: 50

CLI snippets

# view tenant slice status
redwoodctl tenant-slice describe --tenant payments --region us-west-2

# deduct burst credits (operator)
redwoodctl tenant-slice adjust-burst --tenant payments --amount -200

SLOs and alerting thresholds

Primary SLOs (per-tenant):
- P95 latency <= configured SLO (default 150ms for priority slices)
- Error rate (5xx + model-runtime-exceeded) < 0.5%
- Burst credit exhaustion events per week <= 2 for priority tenants

Dashboard panels to create:
- Per-tenant P95/P99 latency heatmap (by model variant)
- Burst credit balance over time (alert when < 20%)
- Tail queue length and number of evictions last 1h

Alert rules (examples):
- SEV2: tenant_p95 > SLO for 10m AND queue_len > 5 -> notify oncall + paging
- SEV3: burst_credit_balance < 20% -> slack channel warning (no paging)
- SEV1: scheduler restarting more than 3 times in 5m -> page SRE

Eviction and fallback chain (playbook)

1) Detection
- router-service emits queue_len and token_age metrics. Anomaly triggers SEV2.

2) Automated actions (fast path)
- If queue_len > threshold && burst_credit_balance == 0 -> apply fallback_model_variant for 60s window.
- Autoscaler attempts to add one node (if Dedicated and pool has capacity) and extend burst credits if finance policy allows.

3) Operator actions (if automated actions fail)
- Run: redwoodctl pool scale --pool payments-priority --delta 1
- If scale blocked, move tenants to reserved_fallback_pool: redwoodctl tenant-slice migrate --tenant payments --target reserved-fallback

4) Post-incident
- Run chargeback reconciliation and mark incident in incident tracker.
- Replenish burst credits and run retrospective checklist below.

Runbook: immediate checklist (ordered)

1. Acknowledge alert and set bridge link.
2. Identify impacted tenant(s) and current slice config (redwoodctl tenant-slice describe).
3. Check burst_credit_balance and queue_len panels.
4. Execute automated fallback if not already applied (see automated actions).
5. If SEV1 conditions, page SRE and escalate to platform leads.

Rollout and testing plan

1) Canary (internal): enable priority slice configs for 3 internal tenants. Observe for 72h.
2) Synthetic load test: run 1x and 10x baseline traffic for 30m. Validate: no silent increases in token cost, queue_len remains bounded.
3) Customer pilot: pick 2 low-risk customers, offer priority slices with explicit burst-credit contract.
4) GA: enable self-serve in Console and guardrails for minimum commit.

Feature flag / migration snippet

# feature flags used in rollout
- ff.tenant-slice-v2: controls new burst-credit accounting
- ff.fallback-chain-v3: turns on model-variant fallback controller

Retrospective template (post-incident)

- Summary: one-paragraph timeline.
- Root cause: short answer.
- Contributing factors: list.
- Action items (owner, due date, status).
- Economic impact: estimate added compute hours and burst-credit usage.
- Customer impact: list affected tenants and messages sent.

Ownership and contacts

- Platform SRE: Ethan Zhao (pager: @ethan, escalation Slack: #sre-oncall)
- Serving Runtime Lead: Priya Raman
- Product / Billing: Marta Kaczmarek

Appendix: common failure modes and mitigations

1) Silent burst credit drain
- Symptom: burst_credit_balance drops rapidly while throughput steady.
- Likely cause: hot prefix cache misses, leading to increased model compute.
- Mitigation: increase per-tenant prefix cache TTL and validate cache hit rate; temporarily raise baseline_qps.

2) Eviction thrash
- Symptom: tenants moved repeatedly between pools.
- Cause: mis-tuned eviction hysteresis.
- Mitigation: set min_stable_window=10m, require 2 consecutive breach windows before eviction.

3) Fallback model quality regression
- Symptom: outputs fail evals post-fallback.
- Cause: fallback order not quality-validated for tenant prompts.
- Mitigation: maintain per-tenant eval promptset and run nightly quality check on candidate fallback variants.

References and links

- Runtime SLOs: /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/tail-latency-visibility-and-mitigation-roadmap-2027 (internal)
- Billing primitives: /confluence/finance-and-legal/contracts-and-legal-process/chargeback-models-2025

Notes

This document is intentionally prescriptive: keep isolation decisions data-driven (use cost-per-token and P95 impact) and prefer soft isolation with verified fallback chains before committing to expensive reserved capacity. Update this playbook when: we add a new model variant, change burst accounting, or introduce a new scheduler heuristic.
